reason: The differentiation signals select the stem-cell descendants that can become muscle precursors, a necessary starting point for the fibre.
expectation: The population will develop muscle precursors that can subsequently fuse.

effect: The signals produced myoblasts that make contractile and fusion proteins, so the next step is to join them.
reaction: The contrast with collagen-secreting fibroblasts makes their different roles clear.
reason: The fusion proteins match the membranes of adjacent myoblasts and should join the precursors into a muscle fibre.
expectation: The myoblasts will fuse into a long cell containing multiple nuclei.

effect: Fusion produced a multinucleated fibre with assembled filaments; the covered actin sites suggest it now needs the calcium signal.
reaction: The one-cell outline makes the relationship between fusion and multiple nuclei clear.
reason: The calcium pulse is the available signal for activating the fibre's pulling machinery.
expectation: Calcium will uncover actin's binding sites so myosin can pull on the filaments.

effect: Calcium exposed the binding sites and enabled filament sliding; the fibre now needs calcium returned to storage to become ready again.
reaction: The distinction between sliding filaments and shortening filaments is clear.
reason: The calcium-pumping membranes should remove the activating calcium from around the filaments.
expectation: ATP-powered pumps will return calcium to storage, allowing the fibre to relax and become ready again.

effect: Calcium pumping stopped the pull and completed the fibre goal; the next task is to assemble and attach the muscles.
reaction: It is useful to see that calcium removal requires ATP and that an outside pull lengthens the fibre.
reason: The empty biceps sheaths need muscle fibres to form the muscle.
expectation: The fibres will fill the biceps sheaths and connect to their tendon routes.

alternatives.reason: The triceps also needs fibres, so it could be built first instead.

effect: The fibres first needed extracellular matrix to form fascicles; there are enough bundles for both muscles.
reaction: The connective layers clarify how individual fibres are grouped, though I had missed that intermediate step.
reason: The biceps sheaths have empty muscle-head spaces that the fascicles can fill.
expectation: The fascicles will form the biceps within its sheaths and tendon routes.

effect: The fascicles formed the two biceps heads, with connective tissue linking fibre force to the tendons.
reaction: The force-transfer inset makes the sheaths' purpose clearer.
reason: The biceps tendons are positioned toward the shoulder and radius, so the movable skeleton is the natural attachment target.
expectation: The biceps tendons will attach across the elbow to the arm skeleton.

alternatives.reason: I could check its available partners, but its tendon routes suggest the skeleton.

effect: The biceps is attached and flexes the elbow; the assembly still needs an extensor.
reaction: The two poses clarify how the biceps pulls on the radius.
reason: The remaining fascicles should fill the triceps sheaths to make the opposing muscle.
expectation: The fascicles will form a triceps with tendons ready to attach to the arm.

effect: The remaining fascicles formed the triceps, ready to fill the arm assembly’s extensor slot.
reaction: The three-head cutaway distinguishes the triceps’ attachment routes.
reason: The triceps is the missing extensor, and its tendon reaches the ulna across the elbow.
expectation: The triceps will attach to the arm assembly and provide elbow extension.

effect: The triceps filled the extensor slot, completing the arm and showing how attachment positions turn similar muscle pulls into opposite elbow movements.
reaction: The paired flexion and extension poses make the contrast clear.

mostWorthwhile.text: Building and attaching both muscles connected the microscopic pulling machinery to movement at the elbow; the planned force-transfer inset also explained the role of connective tissue and tendons.

leastWorthwhile.text: The initial attempt to put fibres directly into the biceps sheaths was a detour, although the automatic fascicle construction made the missing intermediate useful.

surprise.text: The relaxation step made clear that ATP is needed to pump calcium back into storage, while an outside pull lengthens the fibre.

arbitrary.text: The need to form fascicles before filling the sheaths was not obvious to me at first, but the resulting picture explained the connective layers and their purpose.

continue.text: I would choose to continue: connecting cell-level mechanisms to the completed elbow assembly was worthwhile, though the sequence was mostly predictable.
